# About this practical {#sec-about}

This document is the hands-on companion to the chapter *Linear Regression Analysis in Health and Medicine*. The chapter develops the theory and hides the code; this practical shows the code and keeps the theory to the minimum needed to justify each step. Where a concept needs more than a sentence, the chapter is the place to go.

It is written for postgraduate students in public health and epidemiology who already use R at a basic level — you can install a package, run a script and read a data frame — and who now want to carry out a linear regression analysis properly, from raw file to reportable table.

## The REAAAPP workflow

Every analysis in this document follows **REAAAPP**, the workflow used in our teaching. The value of a named workflow is that it forces the unglamorous steps — exploring the data, stating the assumptions, assessing the fitted model — to happen *before* the results are written up, rather than being retrofitted when a reviewer asks.

| Step | Stands for | What you do |
|:---|:---|:-------------|
| **Preparation** | Prepare | Load the packages you will need |
| **R** | Read | Read the data into R and make the column names clean |
| **E** | Explore | Plot and tabulate. Flag anything suspicious — do not act on it yet |
| **A** | Assume | State the distributional assumption the method requires |
| **A** | Apply | Fit the models: simple, then multiple, then interaction |
| **A** | Assess | Check the fitted model against its assumptions, look for what the model left out, and list the outliers and influential points |
| **P** | Present | Produce the tables and figures a reader will actually see, including a sensitivity fit |
| **P** | Publish | Put the document and the code where others can reach them |

: The REAAAPP workflow {tbl-colwidths="[12,15,73]"}

## Why tidy principles

Three habits carry this entire document, and they are worth naming before you meet them:

1. **Tidy data.** One row per observation, one column per variable. The MSSM data already arrives in this shape, which is why almost no reshaping is needed.
2. **Verbs that return data frames.** `filter()`, `mutate()`, `select()`, `summarise()` all take a data frame and give one back, so they compose with the pipe (`|>`) and can be read left to right as a sentence.
3. **Tidy model output.** A fitted `lm` object is a list, not a table — awkward to filter, sort or plot. `broom::tidy()` turns it into a data frame with one row per coefficient, and `broom::glance()` gives one row per model. Once model output is rectangular, you can run eighteen regressions and handle the results with the same verbs you use on the raw data. Section [-@sec-slr] does exactly that.

# Preparation {#sec-prep}

`pacman::p_load()` installs a package if it is missing and loads it if it is not, so a colleague can run this document without hunting through error messages.

```{r}
#| label: setup-packages

if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman")
}

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse, # dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, purrr, forcats, stringr
  haven, # readers for SPSS, Stata and SAS files
  here, # file paths that do not break when the working directory moves
  gtsummary, # publication-ready summary and regression tables
  DT, # interactive HTML tables
  readxl, # reader for Excel files
  janitor, # clean_names() and other data-cleaning helpers
  broom, # tidy(), glance() and augment() for model output
  car, # vif()
  lmtest, # bptest()
  emmeans, # estimated marginal means and simple slopes
  patchwork, # combine ggplot objects into panels
  knitr # kable()
)
```

`haven` is part of the standard workflow because health data so often arrives as `.sav` or `.dta`. This particular dataset is an Excel workbook, so `readxl::read_excel()` does the reading; `haven` is loaded here only so that the habit stays intact.

A few global settings, so that every plot and table in the document looks the same:

```{r}
#| label: setup-options

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
theme_gtsummary_compact()
set.seed(2026)

# One p-value format for every hand-built table in this document. Rounding a
# p-value of 1e-50 to three decimals would print 0.000, which is never correct.
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
}

# here::i_am() tells the here package which file it is looking at, so that
# here() resolves to the project root rather than to the practical/ folder.
here::i_am("practical/mssm_linear_regression_practical.qmd")
```

# R — Read the data {#sec-read}

## Reading the file

The data come from the **Metabolic Syndrome Study in Malaysia (MSSM)**, a cross-sectional study of adults. The outcome throughout is **fasting blood sugar in mmol/L**.

```{r}
#| label: read-raw

raw <- read_excel(here::here("dataset", "mssm_fasting_blood_sugar.xlsx"))

dim(raw)
```

## Cleaning the column names

Raw column names in health datasets are rarely usable. This file mixes capitalisation, spaces, brackets and units:

```{r}
#| label: names-before

names(raw)[c(3, 8, 12, 20)]
```

A name containing a space or a bracket has to be back-quoted every time you use it, which is a permanent source of typing errors. `janitor::clean_names()` converts every name to lower-case snake case in one call. **Do this immediately after reading, before anything else touches the data.**

```{r}
#| label: names-after

raw <- clean_names(raw)
names(raw)[c(3, 8, 12, 20)]
```

## Deriving, recoding and selecting

Now one pipeline does the rest of the preparation. Read it top to bottom as a sequence of instructions:

```{r}
#| label: prepare-data

dat <- raw |>
  # 1. derive the two anthropometric indices that are not in the file
  mutate(
    bmi = weight_kg / (height_m^2), # kg/m^2
    whr = waist_cm / hip_circum_cm # unitless
  ) |>
  # 2. the categorical variables arrive as character; regression needs factors
  mutate(across(c(ruralurban, malefemale, race, marital, hx_dm2), as.factor)) |>
  # 3. set the reference level of each factor explicitly, never by accident
  mutate(
    race = fct_relevel(race, "malay"),
    ruralurban = fct_relevel(ruralurban, "rural"),
    hx_dm2 = fct_relevel(hx_dm2, "no"),
    malefemale = fct_relevel(malefemale, "female"),
    marital = fct_relevel(marital, "married")
  ) |>
  # 4. give the outcome a short name
  rename(fbs = fasting_blood_sugar) |>
  # 5. keep only what the analysis needs
  select(
    fbs,
    age,
    height_m,
    weight_kg,
    waist_cm,
    hip_circum_cm,
    neck_circum_cm,
    bmi,
    whr,
    sbp1,
    dbp1,
    total_bilirubin,
    total_cholesterol,
    fasting_tg,
    ruralurban,
    malefemale,
    race,
    marital,
    hx_dm2
  )

glimpse(dat)
```

Three points deserve emphasis, because each is a common source of a wrong answer later.

**Derived variables are computed once, in the data pipeline, not inside the model formula.** Body mass index and waist–hip ratio are

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{weight (kg)}}{[\text{height (m)}]^2}, \qquad \text{WHR} = \frac{\text{waist (cm)}}{\text{hip (cm)}}.$$

Computing them here means every table, plot and model uses the same definition.

**Character columns must become factors.** `lm()` will coerce a character vector for you, but it will choose the reference level alphabetically and silently.

**Reference levels are a modelling decision, not a default.** Every coefficient for a categorical variable is a comparison *against the reference level*, so the reference determines what the numbers mean. Here Malay is the reference ethnicity because it is the largest group, rural is the reference for residence, and "no" is the reference for a history of type 2 diabetes so that the coefficient reads as the effect of *having* a history.

```{r}
#| label: check-reference-levels

dat |>
  select(where(is.factor)) |>
  map(levels)
```

The first level listed for each variable is its reference.
